presentingComplaint: Found unresponsive with slow, shallow breathing at home
history: Brought in by paramedics after being found unrousable in his bedroom by a flatmate. A used syringe and spoon were beside him. Known history of injection heroin use with two prior non-fatal overdoses; recently released from a 3-week inpatient detox programme (loss of tolerance). No preceding trauma, seizure, or febrile illness. No chronic cardiorespiratory disease.
examination: Pinpoint pupils (miosis) bilaterally, reactive but sluggish. GCS 7 (E1 V2 M4), unrousable to voice, localizes to pain. Respirations slow and shallow with intermittent apnoeic pauses; cyanosis of lips. No focal neurological deficit, no neck stiffness, no rash. Fresh needle-track marks over both antecubital fossae. Chest clear, no crepitations. Abdomen soft. Afebrile, no signs of infection.

labs.ABG: pH 7.24, PaCO2 8.9 kPa (67 mmHg), PaO2 7.8 kPa on room air - acute respiratory acidosis
labs.urine toxicology: positive for opioids, negative for benzodiazepines and stimulants

imaging: CXR normal, no aspiration or pulmonary oedema. CT head (done after partial reversal, to exclude structural cause) - normal.
finalDiagnosis: Acute opioid overdose (heroin) with respiratory depression
citations: Harrison 22e - Opioid Use Disorder and Opioid Intoxication/Overdose
contraindications: Naloxone precipitates acute withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients - titrate in small increments (40-100 mcg IV) to restore adequate ventilation, not full arousal
Avoid over-reversal in chronic users to prevent agitation, vomiting/aspiration, and flash pulmonary oedema
Short naloxone half-life (~30-90 min) < many opioids - mandatory observation and possible re-dosing/infusion
edgeCases: Long-acting or extended-release opioids (methadone, sustained-release oxycodone) may re-sedate hours after naloxone wears off
Co-ingestion with benzodiazepines or alcohol blunts the classic pinpoint-pupil response and prolongs sedation
Body-packer/stuffer rupture can cause recurrent overdose despite reversal
expectedMaiK: Classic opioid toxidrome - depressed consciousness, bradypnoea and miosis after injection heroin with lost tolerance post-detox. Priority is airway/ventilation support plus titrated naloxone; anticipate re-sedation because naloxone is shorter-acting than the opioid, so observe for a prolonged period rather than discharging early.
expectedNextQuestions: What and how much was taken, and was any long-acting opioid (methadone/MR oxycodone) or co-ingestant (benzodiazepine/alcohol) involved?
How did he respond to naloxone, and has sedation recurred as it wears off?
expectedInvestigations: Titrated IV/IM naloxone with response monitoring
Urine toxicology and paracetamol/salicylate levels to exclude co-ingestion
regressionAssertions: miosisSecretions + bradypnea + drugOverdose must map to opioid toxidrome, not organophosphate
